issues.issue: The execution date is incomplete — "on the Ist day of ____ 1999" leaves the month blank, so the date the Agreement was made cannot be fixed from its own words. That matters because Section 11 purports to give it an effective date years earlier.

The enumerated custodial services (hold, settle, collect income, deliver on written direction) contain no authority to lend the Owner's securities, which cannot be squared with Section 1 of the Securities Lending Agreement reciting that the custody agreements "authorize Participant to appoint an agent to lend securities from the Account."

Subparagraph (b), "Act upon written direction from the Owner or from one or more investment managers duly appointed in writing by the Owner," does not say whether such direction can enlarge the Custodian's listed duties or who qualifies as a duly appointed manager. The recital names Julius Baer as the adviser, leaving the class otherwise undefined.

The enumerated powers — nominee holding, employment of agents for ministerial and non-discretionary duties, and execution of transfer documents — omit any power to lend account securities or to act as lending agent, which cannot be squared with Section 1 of the Securities Lending Agreement assuming such authority exists in the custody agreements.

Subparagraph (c)'s catch-all — "any other instruments that may be necessary or appropriate to carry out the custodianship duties and powers" — sits against the specific enumeration and invites an ejusdem generis fight over how far it reaches. "Necessary or appropriate" has no stated benchmark.

The duty to report "an inventory of assets in the account, all activity during the previous month, and a market value for the assets" does not square with Section 6 of the Securities Lending Agreement, under which the Bank keeps security loan records separate from the custodial portfolio records. Whether loaned securities and cash-collateral investments must appear on the monthly custody statement is left open.

"Such other reports as the Owners may reasonably request" and "as may be necessary" set no boundary on subject matter, frequency or cost, and "reasonably" is measured against nothing. Whether the Owner could demand reports on securities-lending collateral investments under this sentence is undeterminable from its words.

Compensation is "as set forth in Schedule A," but no Schedule A is attached to the instrument and the clause supplies no mechanism for what governs in its absence. "As amended from time to time by the parties" also leaves unclear whether a fee change needs the writing that Section 6 requires for amendments.

The modifier is misplaced: "out-of-pocket expenses during the reasonable performance of the Custodian's duties" makes "reasonable" qualify performance rather than the expenses, so it is unclear whether unreasonable expenses are reimbursable. "Out-of-pocket" is itself undefined.

The clause requires lists of authorized persons but states no consequence if a list is never furnished, and it cannot easily be squared with Section 1(b), under which the Custodian acts on direction from managers "duly appointed in writing." Whether the Custodian may act for a manager whose list is missing is left unresolved.

"Entitled to rely on the oral advice as confirmed in writing or written advice of such persons" is ambiguous as to whether written confirmation is a condition of reliance on oral advice or merely a later formality. The phrase can be read either way on its face.

Reliance on oral advice cannot be squared with Section 1(b), (c), (g) and (h), which require the Custodian to act, settle and deliver only on written direction of the Owner or an appointed manager. Which sentence governs an oral instruction to deliver securities is unresolved.

The written-amendment requirement is in tension with Section 4, which lets Schedule A be "amended from time to time by the parties" without saying a writing is needed, and raises the question whether the later Securities Lending Agreement amended this custody arrangement. Neither instrument says which controls.

The 30-day termination notice cannot be squared with Section 9 of the Securities Lending Agreement, which requires 60 days written notice to terminate the lending relationship built on this same account. Terminating custody on 30 days leaves the lending agency's status undetermined.

The unqualified duty to deliver "all securities held in the account" on termination cannot be performed as to securities out on loan, and conflicts with Section 4 of the Securities Lending Agreement, which gives the Bank a reasonable time to liquidate cash collateral investments before terminating a loan. Nothing here says what happens to loaned securities on termination.

"Any fees remaining outstanding and balances owing to the Custodian" is undefined — "balances owing" could mean unreimbursed expenses, overdrafts, or amounts owed under other agreements such as the securities lending program. The clause also gives no valuation or notice mechanism for the assets withheld.

The carve-out — "in the event Custodian has committed negligence or malfeasance ... the indemnification provisions of the Agreement shall not apply" — does not say whether it defeats the indemnity only as to the negligent act or as to the whole claim, and "malfeasance" is undefined. "Any and all claims, liabilities, and expenses" in the first sentence is correspondingly open-ended.

By disapplying "the indemnification provisions of the Agreement," the carve-out may be read to reach Section 21, the Custodian's own indemnity of the Owner, rather than only this section. The two indemnities are not reconciled anywhere in the instrument.

The unconditional right of the Owner to examine records "relevant to this Agreement" cannot be squared with Section 17, which permits examination only on the Custodian's premises, during business hours, and only upon written instructions from an appropriate officer of the Owner. Which set of conditions governs an inspection demand is unresolved.

Colorado law governing "all transactions hereunder" cannot be squared with Section 12 of the Securities Lending Agreement, which applies Minnesota law to lending transactions in this same account. Which law governs a claim arising from lending of custodied assets is left open.
